title: Screen or Classroom?
intro: Millions of students have now studied both online and in a classroom. Which way of learning works better?

passage: In the spring of 2020, something happened that nobody had planned. As the COVID-19 pandemic spread, schools and universities in many countries closed their doors, and more than a billion students suddenly had to learn from home. Teachers who had never used video software were giving lessons through a laptop camera, and children were doing their homework on their parents' phones. It was the largest experiment in online education that the world had ever seen.

Online learning was not completely new, of course. Universities had offered distance courses for many years, and in 2012 several websites began to offer free online courses from well-known universities, which anyone with an internet connection could join. These courses attracted millions of learners. However, researchers soon noticed a problem: only a small percentage of the people who signed up actually completed them.

For many learners, the biggest advantage of studying online is flexibility. A nurse who works at night can watch a lecture in the afternoon, and a student in a small village can take a course from a university on the other side of the world. Online lessons can also be recorded, so learners are able to pause, go back and listen again when something is difficult. For shy students, writing a question in a chat box may feel much easier than raising a hand in front of thirty classmates.

On the other hand, learning at home requires a lot of self-discipline. Without a teacher in the room, it is easy to open a new window and start watching videos instead of listening. During the school closures, many teachers reported that their students had fallen behind, especially younger children and those from poorer families, who often did not have a quiet place to study or a reliable internet connection. For these students, the gap between them and their classmates grew wider.

Classrooms offer something that is difficult to copy on a screen: human contact. In a real classroom, a teacher can see immediately when a student looks confused and can explain the idea in a different way. Students also learn from each other, whether they are working on a group project or simply chatting in the corridor between lessons. Many young people said that during the lockdowns they missed their friends more than anything else, and some experts believe that this lack of contact affected their mental health.

So which is better? Most educators now agree that the answer is not one or the other. Many schools and universities have moved towards 'blended learning', in which students attend some lessons in person and complete other activities online. If it is planned well, this approach can combine the convenience of technology with the motivation that comes from being part of a real community. The pandemic showed that screens can never fully replace teachers, but it also proved that they can be a powerful tool.

A mix of both ways of learning can work best.
Online learning is better for most students.
